cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: chi-squared test of independence on a 3x2 agree/neutral/disagree by men/women table
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.0003082 and states the underlying statistic is 16.16957 with 2 degrees of freedom. cases.description: Actual and expected ranges identical, so the chi-squared statistic is exactly 0

This case checks the documented statistic definition at its degenerate point without depending on any published figure

cases.description: Existence probe only: COPILOT sends a prompt to an Azure-hosted AI model, so its output is neither deterministic nor reproducible; this case only records whether the engine recognizes the function name at all
cases.expected_note: NOT ASSERTABLE BY DESIGN, and deliberately recorded as a probe rather than a support claim. Microsoft's page states the function "calls an AI model hosted on Azure directly from a cell formula", requires an active internet connection and a qualifying Copilot licence, currently uses gpt-4.1-mini (2025-04-14), and that "formula results may change over time, even with the same arguments" -- so there is no value any engine could be held to. The page also announces that from 2026-09-14 the COPILOT function will no longer be available in Excel at all. Without a licence Excel itself documents #BLOCKED ("License Not Found"), so a non-Excel engine returning #NAME? tells us the name is unknown, which is the only comparable datum here

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the cosine of 1.047 radians
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5001711. Independently derived: math.cos(1.047) = 0.5001710745970701 -> 0.5001711 at 7 dp. 1.047 is a decimal approximation of pi/3, which is why the result sits just above 0.5

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 60 degrees converted to radians by multiplying by PI()/180
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5, and cos(60 degrees) = cos(pi/3) = 1/2 exactly. In IEEE double arithmetic math.cos(math.pi/3) evaluates to 0.5000000000000001, one unit in the last place above 0.5, so the assertion is made at 9 dp where the exact and floating-point values agree

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the same 60 degrees converted with the RADIANS function instead
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5 as well. Exactly the same mathematics as the previous case; the point of running both is that Excel documents RADIANS and the explicit PI()/180 multiplication as interchangeable, so a divergence between the two rows would be an engine quirk in RADIANS rather than in COS

cases.description: The cosine at zero
cases.expected_note: Follows from the definition of the cosine, cos(0) = 1 exactly, with no rounding needed: this anchors the function at a point where any floating-point implementation must be exact

cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 27.308233. Independently derived from the documented formula cosh(x) = (e^x + e^-x)/2: math.cosh(4) = 27.308232836016487, and (math.exp(4)+math.exp(-4))/2 gives the same to machine precision -> 27.308233 at 6 dp

cases.description: The hyperbolic cosine at zero

cases.description: The hyperbolic cosine of -4, which must equal that of +4
cases.expected_note: cosh is an even function: the documented formula (e^x + e^-x)/2 is unchanged when x is replaced by -x, so COSH(-4) must return exactly the documented COSH(4) value of 27.308233. Verified independently: math.cosh(-4) = 27.308232836016487, bit-identical to math.cosh(4)

cases.description: The cotangent at zero

EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds return #NUM! here, i.e. they collapse the two documented error classes onto the out-of-range one

cases.description: An argument at the documented magnitude limit of 2^27
cases.expected_note: Excel documents: "The absolute value of Number must be less than 2^27" and "If Number is outside its constraints, COT returns the #NUM! error value." 2^27 = 134217728 is exactly the excluded boundary. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds ignore this range check and return -0.846108835418734 instead of the documented error -- and that number is not garbage: cot(2^27) re-derived with mpmath at 60 digits is -0.84610883541873383485, so LibreOffice's argument reduction is accurate to full double precision here and it simply declines to refuse an input Excel refuses

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the hyperbolic cotangent of 2
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result to three decimals as 1.037. Independently derived from the documented relationship coth(x) = 1/tanh(x) = (e^x + e^-x)/(e^x - e^-x): 1/math.tanh(2) = 1.0373147207275482 -> 1.037314721 at 9 dp, agreeing with the published 1.037 at the depth the page prints

cases.description: The hyperbolic cotangent of -2, which must be the negative of that of +2
cases.expected_note: coth is an odd function: (e^-x + e^x)/(e^-x - e^x) is the negative of (e^x + e^-x)/(e^x - e^-x), so COTH(-2) must be exactly -COTH(2). Verified independently: 1/math.tanh(-2) = -1.0373147207275482

cases.description: An argument at the documented magnitude limit of 2^27

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: days from the start of the coupon period to settlement, semiannual, actual/actual
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 71. Setup serials are the dates Microsoft's page prints: 40568 = 2011-01-25 (settlement), 40862 = 2011-11-15 (maturity), frequency 2 (semiannual), basis 1 (actual/actual). Counting coupon dates back from maturity in six-month steps gives 2011-11-15, 2011-05-15, 2010-11-15, so the settlement date falls in the coupon period 2010-11-15 to 2011-05-15. On basis 1 the count is the actual number of days from 2010-11-15 to 2011-01-25: 15 remaining days in November + 31 in December + 25 in January = 71, confirmed by Python date subtraction

cases.description: The same bond on the US (NASD) 30/360 basis instead of actual/actual

This case discriminates the basis argument, which the documented example alone does not

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: smallest k whose cumulative binomial probability over 6 fair trials reaches 0.75
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 4. Independently derived by summing the binomial probabilities explicitly: with trials 6 and probability 0.5 the cumulative sums are 0.015625, 0.109375, 0.34375, 0.65625, 0.890625, 0.984375, 1.0 for k = 0..6. The first sum that is >= the criterion 0.75 is 0.890625 at k = 4, which is the documented answer

cases.description: The same trials and probability at a stricter criterion of 0.9
cases.expected_note: From the same explicit cumulative sums, the first value >= 0.9 is 0.984375 at k = 5 (the cumulative sum at k = 4 is 0.890625, just short). This case discriminates the alpha argument and pins the >= comparison direction

cases.description: A non-integer number of trials, which the documentation says is truncated
cases.expected_note: Excel documents "If trials is not an integer, it is truncated", so 6.9 must behave exactly as 6. With 6 trials the cumulative sums are 0.015625, 0.109375, 0.34375, 0.65625, ...; the first one >= the criterion 0.6 is 0.65625 at k = 3. The criterion 0.6 was chosen precisely because it discriminates: with 7 trials the sums are 0.0078125, 0.0625, 0.2265625, 0.5, 0.7734375, ... and the first >= 0.6 is at k = 4, so an engine that rounded 6.9 up to 7 instead of truncating would return 4 here. (At the page's own criterion of 0.75 both 6 and 7 trials give 4, which is why this case does not reuse it)

cases.description: A success probability of exactly 0
cases.expected_note: Excel documents: "If probability_s is <= 0 or probability_s => 1, CRITBINOM returns the #NUM! error value." The same silent substitution was already recorded for CRITBINOM's modern replacement BINOM.INV elsewhere in this corpus, so it is the function family's behaviour and not a one-off

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the cosecant of 15 radians
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result to three decimals as 1.538. Independently derived from the documented identity CSC(n) = 1/SIN(n): 1/math.sin(15) = 1.5377805615408537 -> 1.537780562 at 9 dp, agreeing with the published 1.538. The argument is 15 RADIANS, not degrees

cases.description: The cosecant of -15, which must be the negative of that of +15
cases.expected_note: sin is odd, so by the documented identity CSC(n) = 1/SIN(n) the cosecant is odd too: CSC(-15) must be exactly -CSC(15). Verified independently: 1/math.sin(-15) = -1.5377805615408537

cases.description: An argument at the documented magnitude limit of 2^27
cases.expected_note: Excel documents: "The absolute value of Number must be less than 2^27" and "If Number is outside its constraints, CSC returns the #NUM! error value." 2^27 = 134217728 is exactly the excluded boundary. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds return -1.30992372349448 instead of the documented error; csc(2^27) re-derived with mpmath at 60 digits is -1.3099237234944811929, so the value is correct to full double precision and only the documented range check is missing

cases.description: A non-numeric argument
cases.expected_note: Excel documents: "If Number is a non-numeric value, CSC returns the #VALUE! error value."

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the hyperbolic cosecant of 1.5
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result to four decimals as 0.4696. Independently derived from csch(x) = 1/sinh(x) = 2/(e^x - e^-x): 1/math.sinh(1.5) = 0.46964244059522464 -> 0.469642441 at 9 dp, agreeing with the published 0.4696

cases.description: The hyperbolic cosecant of -1.5, which must be the negative of that of +1.5
cases.expected_note: sinh is odd, so csch = 1/sinh is odd as well: CSCH(-1.5) must be exactly -CSCH(1.5). Verified independently: 1/math.sinh(-1.5) = -0.46964244059522464

cases.description: An argument at the documented magnitude limit of 2^27
cases.expected_note: Excel documents: "The absolute value of Number must be less than 2^27" and "If Number is outside its constraints, CSCH returns the #NUM! error value." 2^27 = 134217728 is exactly the excluded boundary. Mathematically csch(134217728) underflows to 0, so this case tests the documented range check rather than the arithmetic. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds return 0 instead of the documented error, i.e. they answer the mathematics and ignore the range check

cases.description: Existence probe only: the KPI-member form from Microsoft's own example, against a connection name that does not exist in this workbook. No OLAP connection can exist in a flat workbook, so this records what the engine actually returns rather than asserting a documented value
cases.expected_note: NOT EXECUTABLE AS DOCUMENTED, and deliberately recorded as a probe rather than a support claim. Microsoft documents this function as returning data from an OLAP cube reached through a named workbook connection -- the CUBEKPIMEMBER page states outright that the cube functions are "supported only when the workbook is connected to a Microsoft SQL Server 2005 Analysis Services or later data source". A flat .xlsx carries no such connection, and neither LibreOffice Calc nor Google Sheets can supply one, so the documented behaviour cannot be reproduced by this harness in any engine. Microsoft's page documents that "if the connection name is not a valid workbook connection stored in the workbook, CUBEKPIMEMBER returns a #NAME? error value", and the same for an OLAP server that is not running. The trap this case exists to avoid: Excel itself documents that an invalid connection name yields #NAME?, which is the SAME token an engine emits for a function it has never heard of. A #NAME? here therefore does NOT distinguish "present but unconnected" from "absent", and this case is recorded with no asserted expected value so it can never be scored as documented behaviour. What the run does establish is recorded separately: probing all four pinned LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) with the plain name, the _xlfn. storage form and the COM.MICROSOFT. add-in form returned #NAME? for all three spellings on every build, which is the signature of a name the engine does not implement at all rather than of a missing data connection
